tldr: A definitive benchmark that unifies fragmented imitation learning environments for whole-body control into a single API, spanning fast CPU/GPU simulation, automated retargeting, and real-robot deployment.
hero_caption: Twelve humanoid and musculoskeletal models registered in LocoMuJoCo replaying the exact same walking trajectory side by side. A key strength of this benchmark is that models with vastly different body shapes and actuator setups can be handled directly through a shared training loop and dataset interface.
overview:
With the rapid advancement of humanoid robots in recent years, research on acquiring whole-body motions from human motion-capture (mocap) data via imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) has grown increasingly active. However, prior environments have been fragmented across robot-specific codebases, simple locomotion-only tasks, or manipulation-centric domains. Researchers had to rebuild data-processing, retargeting (adapting motions to different body proportions), and evaluation pipelines from scratch whenever they switched robot models.

To solve this, the authors developed "LocoMuJoCo", a comprehensive benchmark that unites CPU-based MuJoCo with GPU-accelerated backends (MJX and MjWarp) under a single unified API. It covers 9 humanoids, 3 biomechanical/musculoskeletal models, and 4 quadrupeds, and features an automated retargeting pipeline that maps human motions to any supported robot.

In experiments, the benchmark demonstrated a massive simulation throughput of up to $4.9 \times 10^5$ steps per second on a single consumer GPU, alongside a large-scale tracking evaluation across 11 robot models and 13 motion clips. Furthermore, via the companion repository "loco-mujoco-real", learned policies were transferred zero-shot to a physical humanoid robot (AgiBot X2 Ultra), stably executing dynamic whole-body motions for 43 seconds.
contributions: Built a unified API that transparently switches between CPU (MuJoCo) and GPU-parallelized environments (MJX/MjWarp) using identical code.

Supported 9 humanoids, 3 musculoskeletal models, and 4 quadrupeds, establishing a retargeting pipeline via the SMPL model that automatically converts motions from human to robot, as well as between robots.

Designed a modular plug-in architecture using Flax dataclasses that completely decouples observations, rewards, control modes, and domain randomizations, making it fully compatible with JAX JIT compilation and parallelization.
Provided an end-to-end pipeline that extends beyond large-scale in-simulation benchmarks to Sim-to-Real deployment on physical humanoid robots.

sections.heading: Unifying fragmented humanoid learning environments
sections.summary: This section highlights how fragmented codebases and evaluation benchmarks have held back humanoid imitation learning. It introduces the background behind LocoMuJoCo, which unites fast GPU-parallel simulation with real-robot deployment.
sections.details:
Humanoid robot hardware is progressing rapidly, making "Sim-to-Real"—deploying policies learned in simulation onto physical hardware—an increasingly practical reality. Because humans and humanoids share similar physical structures, human motion-capture data serves as an invaluable source of supervisory demonstrations.

However, existing imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) benchmarks have remained severely fragmented. They often relied on robot-specific codebases, focused exclusively on manipulation tasks, or were limited to toy flat-ground walking benchmarks. As a result, researchers were repeatedly forced to reimplement data-conversion pipelines, simulator bindings, and evaluation metrics whenever switching to a new target robot.

While the original version of LocoMuJoCo supported only CPU-based MuJoCo, this major update represents a complete JAX-based redesign. By integrating the GPU-parallel execution engines MJX and MjWarp, it has evolved into a one-stop platform covering standard learning algorithms, automated retargeting, and real-world deployment tools.

sections.heading: Combining the best of existing libraries into one unified platform
sections.summary: This section compares the strengths of prior robot and character motion libraries. While each specializes in a narrow domain, LocoMuJoCo is presented as the only platform that simultaneously provides simulator flexibility, automated retargeting, biomechanical models, and real-world robot deployment.
sections.details:
Recent humanoid learning libraries each excel in distinct areas. For instance, HumanoidBench shines in contact-rich reinforcement learning tasks but lacks imitation learning datasets. MyoSuite supports detailed musculoskeletal models but lacks GPU parallelization and Sim-to-Real support. mjlab offers fast simulations via Warp but lacks motion datasets and automated retargeting. Meanwhile, tools like ProtoMotions and MimicKit focus on character animation and tracking algorithms, yet fall short of offering a standardized robotics benchmark.

LocoMuJoCo condenses the core strengths of these existing tools into a single platform. It supports both sequential CPU execution with NumPy and parallel GPU execution with JAX through the exact same API. Simultaneously, it provides automated motion retargeting for every registered robot, biomechanical musculoskeletal models, trajectory similarity metrics, and a full Sim-to-Real transfer pipeline.

sections.heading: A modular architecture from high-speed GPU execution to real hardware
sections.summary: This section details LocoMuJoCo's internal architecture, supported robots, algorithm implementations, and real-robot workflow. Its stateless plug-in design maximizes JAX JIT compilation and demonstrates whole-body motion tracking on a physical humanoid.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Dual-Backend Design
Simulations run across two interchangeable backends: a sequential NumPy/MuJoCo backend for CPUs, and a parallel JAX/MJX backend for GPUs. Because JAX syntax mirrors NumPy, environment logic such as observations and rewards is shared across a single codebase without redundant reimplementations. Furthermore, activating the optional MjWarp backend (use_mjwarp=True) achieves an astonishing simulation throughput of up to $4.9 \times 10^5$ environment steps per second on a single consumer GPU.

### 3.2 Fully Modular Plug-in Architecture
Individual environment components—such as observations, rewards, motor or muscle actuations, domain randomizations, terrain generation, and termination conditions—are loosely coupled as independent plug-ins. None of the plug-ins store internal state in global variables; instead, state is passed explicitly between step functions via Flax dataclasses, enabling the entire environment step to be fully JIT-compiled with JAX.

### 3.3 Diverse Robot Models and Automated Retargeting
The library ships with 9 humanoids—including Unitree H1/H1v2/G1, Atlas, Talos, Apollo, Booster T1, ToddlerBot, and Fourier GR1T2—as well as 3 musculoskeletal models and 4 quadrupeds (such as Go2 and Spot). Using the SMPL human body model as an intermediate representation, large-scale mocap datasets like AMASS and LAFAN1 can be automatically retargeted into robot joint trajectories via simple configuration files.

### 3.4 JIT-Optimized Training and Evaluation Infrastructure
A diverse suite of algorithms—including PPO, GAIL, AMP, DeepMimic, the world-model-based SuperMimic, SAC, TD3, and policy distillation pipelines—is compactly implemented in JAX/Flax. Environment stepping and gradient updates are fused into a single JIT loop via lax.scan, eliminating all Python-level overhead.

### 3.5 Seamless Deployment to Physical Humanoids
Through the companion repository "loco-mujoco-real", trained policies can be deployed directly to real-world hardware, including the Unitree G1 and AgiBot X2 Ultra. As shown in Figure F2, a tracking policy trained with domain randomization on the AgiBot X2 Ultra was deployed zero-shot, stably maintaining dynamic whole-body dance motions at 50 Hz for 43 seconds.

captions.F2: Whole-body motion tracking over 43 seconds on the physical humanoid robot AgiBot X2 Ultra. A policy trained using domain randomization on LocoMuJoCo's MjWarp backend was transferred zero-shot to the physical robot, executing smooth and dynamic motions.

sections.heading: Open-source release and a well-maintained codebase
sections.summary: LocoMuJoCo is released fully under the MIT license, complete with robot models, deployment code, and datasets. It achieves 93% test coverage and actively welcomes community contributions.
sections.details:
LocoMuJoCo is open-source under the MIT license on GitHub. The ecosystem includes the core repository (loco-mujoco), loco-mujoco-real for physical deployments, loco-mujoco-models containing robot descriptions, datasets hosted on the Hugging Face Hub, and comprehensive online documentation.

The repository features more than 500 unit tests, reaching 93% code coverage (excluding components that require online asset downloads). Continuous integration (CI) via GitHub Actions ensures high reliability and maintainability across the entire codebase.

sections.heading: Appendix: Three-stage retargeting details and benchmark results
sections.summary: This section covers the three-stage retargeting pipeline using SMPL models, simulation throughput benchmarks, and large-scale experiments across 11 robot embodiments, highlighting close alignment between simulation and real-robot behavior.
sections.details:
### The Three-Stage Retargeting Pipeline
Mapping human motion onto a robot follows three key stages:
- **Stage 1 (Shape Fitting)**: The robot is set to a T-pose, and the SMPL body shape parameters $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ and scale $s$ are optimized via Adam to align with 15 corresponding keypoints (mimic sites). For example, on the Unitree G1, the initial alignment error of 112.1 mm drops significantly to 21.8 mm after optimization.
- **Stage 2 (SMPL-to-Robot Trajectory Generation)**: Using target positions and orientations ($SE(3)$) derived from the fitted SMPL motion trajectory, the robot's joint angle sequence is resolved inversely using MuJoCo equality constraints.
- **Stage 3 (Robot-to-Robot Transfer)**: Trajectories from one robot are projected back onto the SMPL model and then transferred to another target robot. This allows motions to be shared across distinct embodiments without manually repeating marker configurations.

### Simulation Throughput Comparison
In a benchmark on the Unitree G1 with full self-collision checking enabled, MjWarp achieved $4.9 \times 10^5$ steps per second—a 20x to 54x speedup over MJX (around 10k to 25k steps per second). This performance leap stems from MjWarp's broad-phase collision detection, which efficiently culls distant contact candidate pairs.

### Large-Scale Benchmarks and Real-World Validation
Across 11 humanoid models trained on 13 motion clips, combining PPO with DeepMimic consistently yielded the highest episodic returns and tracking accuracy (evaluated using Dynamic Time Warping and Fréchet distance). As shown in Figure F11, the poses in simulation match the physical robot's motions across time with extreme precision, showing that the Sim-to-Real gap remains minimal.

captions.F4: Visualization of the three-stage retargeting pipeline. Left (Stage 1): SMPL body shape is optimized to the robot's T-pose, substantially reducing error. Top-right (Stage 2): SMPL dance motions are converted into robot joint trajectories. Bottom-right (Stage 3): A walking motion from Unitree H1v2 is transferred to Booster T1 via robot-to-robot mapping.
captions.F11: Synchronized time-step comparison of AgiBot X2 Ultra between simulation (left half) and the physical robot (right half). Even during highly dynamic, large-amplitude whole-body poses, simulation and hardware remain closely matched.

takeaways: Human mocap data can be retargeted automatically across differing robot body proportions and kinematic structures simply by defining 15 mimic sites.
Leveraging a stateless JAX/Flax plug-in architecture alongside the MjWarp backend enables ultra-fast parallel training at $4.9 \times 10^5$ steps per second on a single GPU.
Imitation quality can be comprehensively evaluated beyond simulation return using trajectory similarity metrics such as Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) and Fréchet distance.
An official Sim-to-Real pipeline (loco-mujoco-real) allows learned tracking policies to be deployed directly onto physical humanoid robots.
limitations: Users must individually review and comply with licensing terms for commercial use when working with human body models like SMPL and datasets like AMASS.
Real-robot validation was primarily focused on flat-ground tracking tasks; verifying robustness on uneven terrain, stairs, or under heavy external perturbations remains future work.
While the MjWarp backend is exceptionally fast, setting it up can present technical friction due to specific GPU, driver, and MuJoCo version dependencies.
